steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Muslims believe angels (mala'ikah) are created from light and serve as God's messengers. They have no free will — they always obey Allah. Belief in angels is one of the Six Articles of Faith in Sunni Islam.

steps.title: RS Exam Tips — Angels
steps.body: 1. For Angels questions, always include specific scriptural or source references where relevant 2. Explain both religious and non-religious viewpoints 3. Use specialist vocabulary precisely (e.g. terms from the specification) 4. Evaluate by analysing strengths and weaknesses of different views before reaching your conclusion 5. Link your discussion of Angels to its real-world impact on believers and society

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: In the UK, the concept of guardian angels provides comfort to many British Muslims. The belief that two angels record all deeds motivates ethical behaviour: a Muslim knows that even secret actions are witnessed and will be accounted for on the Day of Judgement.

steps.title: UK Context
steps.body: The distinction between angels (who obey perfectly) and humans (who can choose to obey or disobey) is central to the Islamic understanding of morality. Humans are morally superior to angels when they choose good, because their choice involves overcoming temptation — an option angels do not face.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Explain two Muslim beliefs about angels. | "Belief in angels is not important for Muslims today." Evaluate this statement.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Always refer to specific sources of authority (scripture, sacred texts, religious leaders) Explain contrasting beliefs — different views within and between traditions Use key terminology precisely (e.g. tawhid, atonement, sanctity of life) For 12-mark evaluation questions, consider both sides before reaching a justified conclusion Link beliefs to their impact on individuals, communities and society Acknowledge diversity — no religious tradition has a single, uniform view
